# Tech overview {background-color="#001a00"}

::: {.notes}
About 5 minutes.
:::

## The machines

```{=html}
{{< include images/_machines.svg >}}
```

::: {.notes}
Two machines and a tunnel. The laptop runs the browser and TalkWithZombies; the AI runs on a GPU box, a VM on
Hyperstack for the demo, or a home lab PC with a 3090. One command installs the client, one deploys the AI; during the
show, an SSH tunnel brings the box's three services to the laptop's localhost. Where things run, not how the playbook
works (that is the deep dive).

THE LAPTOP — make client-mac (a standalone Ansible playbook that never reads the deployment's inventories): clones
TalkWithZombies at a pinned tag (today tz-0.6) into ~/TalkWithZombies-client, makes a virtual environment, installs the
requirements with pip, and seeds settings.yaml pointing at the tunnel's ports. The app is FastAPI (Python 3.10+),
served on 127.0.0.1:8000. A page on http://localhost counts as a secure context, so the microphone works with no
certificate, domain or TLS. The demo laptop is an M1 with 16 GB: it runs no model. macOS proven; Linux likely, never
tried; Windows unknown.

THE DEPLOY — make ans-deploy ENV=cloud: Ansible over SSH from the laptop. It starts from "an SSH-able Ubuntu box
exists", so nothing is provider-specific. Checks first: the right environment, no placeholder left, Ubuntu, Docker, the
NVIDIA container toolkit, a driver able to run CUDA 12 — it asserts them, never installs them. Then: llama.cpp in a
pinned container (build b11096), Whisper in a container pinned by digest, tts-serve 1.2 as a system service. From zero
in 7 minutes (ok=33 changed=16); the models are about 11 GB to download the first time; a second run reports changed=0
in 30 seconds. The services start again at every boot, and are bound to the box's loopback.

THE TUNNEL — make ssh-tunnel ENV=cloud: one ssh -N with three forwards (llama :8080, tts :8001, whisper :8002),
keepalives every 30 s (it gives up after 3 missed), and it fails at once if a port cannot be forwarded. Security: none
of the services asks for credentials — the SSH key is the whole authentication; the provider's firewall opens only
port 22; the deployment offers only its own key, accepts a new box's host key on first contact and refuses a changed
one, in its own known_hosts (~/.config/zombie-radio/). make check asks the three services for their health through
the tunnel.

THE NETWORK — the laptop sends each line to the voice with the character's reference clip: 590-750 KB per request (WAV,
base64). On a home connection that is lost in about 0.5 s per request; on a slow venue Wi-Fi it could add a second or
more (a compressed-clips switch is a follow-up). Round trip from the laptop to Hyperstack's CANADA-1: about 58 ms.

THE BOX — Hyperstack's RTX A6000, 48 GB, about $0.50-0.59 an hour (provider survey, 2026-09-13); Ubuntu images with
Docker and the NVIDIA toolkit preinstalled. A new VM needs a public IP attached and SSH enabled in the console. A
stopped VM keeps billing; only hibernation stops it — and restoring needs the same GPU in stock, and no process
survives (a full service start). The whole stack uses 14,477 MiB of the 48 GB.

THE HOME PC — the same playbook (make ans-deploy ENV=local) to a Linux desktop with an RTX 3090 (24 GB): Ubuntu
22.04.5, driver R580, Docker with the NVIDIA runtime — the checks passed.
:::

## The components

```{=html}
{{< include images/_components.svg >}}
```

::: {.notes}
The same picture, opened up: the laptop's two parts and the box, the colours the same. A few words on each component.
Three presses of the arrow key: the browser, then the app, then the GPU box.

GBNF = GGML BNF: Backus-Naur Form, the classic notation for grammars, in the dialect of GGML (the tensor library under
llama.cpp). llama.cpp uses it to constrain sampling: at each step, tokens the grammar does not allow are masked out.

THE BROWSER — the page is a small state machine (idle, generating, playing, listening) and it is the show's clock: it
asks for the next round when the voice has drained. Lines arrive as server-sent events while the model writes them.
The voice player cuts each line into chunks of whole sentences (about 100 characters) and plays them in order, each in
the speaker's voice and the line's mood. The microphone is held only while the radio listens: a 10 s window, a press
capped at 30 s. The static bed and the gauge (the magic eye, the oscilloscope) tap the page's audio through Web Audio.
Keys: Space held to talk, M mutes the static, F flips its AM filter. Looks: the 1950 Philips radio and a ham
transmitter, both restyling the same page; /show opens a chooser with live miniatures.

THE APP — TalkWithZombies, our fork of TalkWithMe; the show engine is about 1,900 lines of Python (app/show/), with
1,284 Python tests plus five Node test suites for the page. Three endpoints: /api/show/start (opens a run, picks the
seed), /api/show/round (plans and streams one round), /api/show/listen (transcribes a press).
- The model has no memory between requests: every request carries the whole show so far — the cast sheet as the
  system message (identical each time, so the server's cache serves it), then each round's instruction and the lines
  the model wrote.
- The director plans each round in plain Python. Two modes: Broadcast (the receiver is dead; the cast talk, events
  happen, every 60-180 s of audio the receiver comes back and Samantha calls out) and Contact (the listener speaks; up
  to 5 ± 1 answers, then the receiver breaks down; two silences and it is switched off).
- Every round has an emotional overtone (positive, neutral, negative) that picks its moods, its tone word and its
  event. The story lab-outbreak has 289 events.
- Fixed lines: what the listener must not miss (an event, the call, the breakdown) is said word for word by a cast
  member, not written by the model.
- The grammar allows only the round's speakers, its line count, its moods, and plain text — said in the instruction in
  the same words, so the model is guided, not fought: a grammar that agrees with its prompt costs 0.3-0.5 % per token.
- The trim keeps the script inside the 32k context (deep dive). Whisper's likely inventions — empty text, low
  confidence, known hallucinations — count as silence.
- Every run is recorded in runs/<id>/script.json; with debug on, every prompt, request, reply and voice chunk is kept.
  The seed drives every choice and every model request: the same seed replays the same show on the same box and build.

THE BOX — llama.cpp, tts-serve and Whisper; see "Local AI only" and "The machines".
:::
